documents.title: Using Generative AI Reflectively and Responsibly in Teaching and Learning
tiers: Limited use of AI in class with citation
documents.summary: TLC teaching guide (April 2025) defining GenAI, giving its benefits, harms, and student-use data, and walking instructors through writing and discussing a course policy with three sample syllabus statements. It also addresses accessibility, cost, and licensed tools.
documents.stance_why: The guide sets no rule itself: it tells instructors to 'Make your course’s GenAI policy clear in your syllabus' and offers three example statements (not permitting, limited use with citation, permitting), so the decision is delegated to instructors with tiered options.

units.why: Defines AI as systems that 'perform tasks typically requiring human intellectual activities', which sets what the guide covers (P61).
units.anchor: Artificial intelligence (AI) refers to the development of computer systems

units.why: Defines generative AI as 'a subset of artificial intelligence focused on creating new data', fixing the scope of the guide (P61).
units.anchor: Generative AI (GenAI) is a subset of artificial intelligence focused on creating new data

units.why: States that 'the TLC will update this resource as developments occur', a commitment to revise the guidance (P54).
units.anchor: the TLC will update this resource as developments occur

units.why: Notes GenAI is 'integrated into Google Searches' and tools like Grammarly, widening what counts as GenAI. It is a scope statement (P61); P07 does not fit because no rule about embedded tools is given.
units.anchor: GenAI has also been integrated into Google Searches in the form of AI Overviews
units.fit_note: Says AI is embedded in search and writing tools but sets no rule about them.

units.why: Says 'the university is investing in tools for the community to use' and points to licenses for faculty, staff and students, an institution-wide provision of licensed tools (P92).
units.anchor: the university is investing in tools for the community to use

units.why: Reports UCUES data that '67% of students reported using GenAI tools', evidence on student use (P55).
units.anchor: 67% of students reported using GenAI tools at some point during the academic year
units.frag_start: A majority of UCLA students are

units.why: Reports that 78% of students 'understand how the use of GenAI can be detrimental to their learning', survey evidence about student views (P55).
units.anchor: 78% agree or strongly agree that they understand how the use of GenAI

units.why: Names benefits: 'personalized learning feasible and scalable', a benefit statement (P87) rather than a rule.
units.anchor: making personalized learning feasible and scalable

units.why: Says chatbots and tutors 'may provide more automated grading and feedback', a named benefit (P87).
units.anchor: students to interact with GenAI chatbots and tutors

units.why: Argues 'universities need to teach students how to use GenAI tools effectively and responsibly' because careers will require proficiency, a career-skill rationale (P44).
units.anchor: universities need to teach students how to use GenAI tools effectively and responsibly

units.why: States 'algorithms can and do replicate and produce biased, racist, and sexist outputs', naming bias as a harm (P53).
units.anchor: algorithms can and do replicate and produce biased, racist, and sexist outputs

units.why: Says the technologies 'are not infallible' and may give 'incorrect data' or lack context, a warning about output reliability (P31).
units.anchor: These technologies are not infallible, and their accuracy is subject to a variety of factors
units.frag_end: variety of factors, some listed below:
units.fit_note: Warns about error as a fact; does not tell students to verify.

units.why: Names the data centers' raw materials and 'electronic waste containing mercury and lead' as an environmental concern (P53).
units.anchor: produce electronic waste containing mercury and lead

units.why: Says data centers 'use and will continue to use massive amounts of water', an environmental cost (P53).
units.anchor: Data centers also use and will continue to use massive amounts of water

units.why: Says the 'carbon footprint of a single GenAI query is four to five times higher' than search, an environmental cost (P53).
units.anchor: carbon footprint of a single GenAI query is four to five times higher

units.why: Advises instructors to 'reflect on your views, interest in, and comfort level with GenAI' before setting policy, which is support for faculty to learn about AI first (P63).
units.anchor: reflect on your views, interest in, and comfort level with GenAI

units.why: Offers an 'AI Faculty Consultation Chart' of guiding questions on experience, relevance, ethics and rethinking the course, a faculty support resource (P63).
units.anchor: created a chart with guiding questions for instructors relating to AI

units.why: Tells instructors to 'get in touch with an instructional designer', a consultation service for faculty (P63).
units.anchor: get in touch with an instructional designer to discuss with you

units.why: Suggests a student survey or class discussion about GenAI, so instructors learn what students know and use. It is a discuss-with-students practice (P66).
units.anchor: holding a discussion with your class exploring these topics
units.frag_start: Consider utilizing the questions on AI

units.why: Says the TLC 'created a sample survey' of UCUES questions in Canvas Commons, a ready-made resource for instructors (P63).
units.anchor: We have created a sample survey of these UCUES questions
units.frag_start: We have created a sample survey
units.fit_note: A survey resource instructors can import, not training.

units.why: Directs 'Make your course’s GenAI policy clear in your syllabus', an instruction to state the AI policy in the syllabus (P09).
units.anchor: Make your course’s GenAI policy clear in your syllabus.

units.why: Suggests 'forming a policy in collaboration with your students at the beginning of the quarter', co-creating the policy (P67).
units.anchor: forming a policy in collaboration with your students at the beginning of the quarter
units.frag_end: sense of belonging among students in your course

units.why: The page offers three template statements for instructors to adopt; they are named 'Not permitting', 'Limited use ... with citation' and 'Permitting', which makes three tiers (P05). P04 was considered, but the instructor-choice aspect is carried by the document stance, and here the policy is the named set of options.
units.anchor: three example syllabus statements adapted from UIC’s AI Writing Tools guide
units.frag_end: what to include in your AI statement
units.policy: Offers three named example syllabus statements: not permitting AI, limited use with citation, and permitting AI.

units.why: Template text for the no-AI option: 'is not permitted in this course' bans AI writing tools in the course, a default ban (P01). It is written to students but is sample wording for instructors.
units.anchor: is not permitted in this course
units.frag_start: The use of AI writing tools
units.policy: The use of AI writing tools (including, but not limited to, ChatGPT) is not permitted in this course.

units.why: The no-AI sample gives its reason: students who use the tools 'undermine the goals and learning objectives for this course'. This is a learning rationale (P41), not a fairness one (P95).
units.anchor: undermine the goals and learning objectives for this course

units.why: The no-AI sample says 'Any confirmed use ... will be treated as academic dishonesty', classifying unauthorized AI use as misconduct (P36).
units.anchor: Any confirmed use of AI writing tools will be treated as academic dishonesty

units.why: The limited-use sample says 'Students are encouraged to use AI writing tools ... to generate ideas', an encouraged brainstorming use (P15).
units.anchor: Students are encouraged to use AI writing tools (such as ChatGPT) to generate ideas

units.why: The sample says 'all AI-generated content be reviewed, edited, and verified for accuracy before submission', a duty to verify AI output (P31) that covers every permitted use.
units.anchor: all AI-generated content be reviewed, edited, and verified for accuracy before submission

units.why: The sample says 'you need to cite the specific AI writing tool as a source' when more than one sentence of minimally edited AI text is presented as one's own, a disclosure rule (P24).
units.anchor: you need to cite the specific AI writing tool as a source
units.policy: Students cite the specific AI writing tool as a source if they present more than one sentence of minimally edited AI-generated text as their own.
units.fit_note: Citation is required only above a threshold (more than one sentence of minimally edited AI text); smaller use needs none.

units.why: The limited-use sample justifies permission with 'In order to prepare students for an AI-infused world', a career-preparation rationale (P44).
units.anchor: In order to prepare students for an AI-infused world

units.why: The open sample says AI writing tools are 'permitted in this course with no restrictions', a default permission with no conditions (P02).
units.anchor: the use of AI writing tools is permitted in this course with no restrictions

units.why: The open sample justifies permission with 'prepare students for AI-assisted work', a professional-skill rationale (P44).
units.anchor: In order to prepare students for AI-assisted work

units.why: The open sample adds 'this policy may be revised in light of other policies and novel technological developments', a provisional-policy note (P54).
units.anchor: this policy may be revised in light of other policies and novel technological developments

units.why: Instructors with plagiarism concerns are told 'please follow the Guidance for Addressing Suspected AI Misconduct', a formal procedure to follow (P81), not a classification as misconduct (P36).
units.anchor: please follow the Guidance for Addressing Suspected AI Misconduct

units.why: Instructors are pointed to publishers' statements 'on AI and authorship' (Science, Nature, MLA, APA) as reference points. No type covers using outside authorship norms as a reference, so it is UNCOVERED.
units.anchor: refer to established publications’ statements on AI and authorship
units.uncovered_note: Instructors may consult journal and publisher policies on AI and authorship as a reference when writing their own rules.

units.why: The page links a crowdsourced collection of syllabus policies and invites instructors to 'use them in your syllabus', a form of faculty support. P63 fits only partly since it is a resource list, not a workshop or consultation.
units.anchor: You can read through other educators’ submissions for syllabus statements
units.fit_note: A crowdsourced bank of syllabus statements rather than workshops or consultations.

units.why: Encourages 'conversations with your students about how these tools will support advancements in their field', discussing AI with students (P66).
units.anchor: Have conversations with your students about how these tools will support advancements
units.fit_note: Frames the discussion around the benefits of AI in students' fields.

units.why: Tells instructors to 'Prepare students to thoughtfully engage, co-create, be curious' with GenAI, preparing students for AI-rich work (P44).
units.anchor: Prepare students to thoughtfully engage, co-create, be curious

units.why: Tells instructors to emphasize 'digital literacy, research, and writing skills' when discussing GenAI, and says universities guide AI literacy. This is AI-literacy education (P70).
units.anchor: emphasize the importance of digital literacy, research, and writing skills with students
units.fit_note: Instructor-led literacy emphasis in discussion, not a training program.

units.why: Says the library is 'creating materials for students to learn more about' AI tools and their output, plus a WI+RE tutorial, AI-literacy materials for students (P70).
units.anchor: the library is creating materials for students to learn more about
units.frag_start: In addition, the library is creating
units.frag_end: evaluate AI tools and their output.

units.why: Tells instructors to 'Connect students to library sources for research and writing', directing students to human support (P72).
units.anchor: Connect students to library sources for research and writing

units.why: Tells instructors to 'Facilitate discussions with your students about the impacts of spreading disinformation or biased information'. P66 fits (discuss AI with students) rather than P53, which names harms but does not tell instructors to discuss them.
units.anchor: Facilitate discussions with your students about the impacts of spreading disinformation or biased information

units.why: Warns GenAI tools 'may not always be accessible to individuals with disabilities', an accessibility concern (P97).
units.anchor: GenAI tools may not always be accessible to individuals with disabilities

units.why: Tells instructors to 'Open a conversation with the Center for Accessible Education' about accessible alternatives, an accessibility step (P97).
units.anchor: Open a conversation with the Center for Accessible Education (CAE)

units.why: Encourages faculty to use a syllabus statement 'to direct a student toward CAE', pointing students to human support for accommodations (P72); P51 is also related but P72 states the referral itself.
units.anchor: Faculty are encouraged to use this suggested syllabus statement to direct a student toward CAE
units.frag_start: Faculty are encouraged to use this
units.frag_end: listed Disability Specialist on their accommodation letter.

units.why: Says GenAI 'subscriptions come at a cost, so continuing to revisit your learning goals and activities with respect to access is a critical equity issue', an access and cost concern (P51).
units.anchor: Some GenAI tools and subscriptions come at a cost

units.why: Says 'Using UCLA’s available GenAI tools ensures that the technology does not come at a cost to students', free access is provided (P51).
units.anchor: ensures that the technology does not come at a cost to students

units.why: Notes 'only students 18 and older can use these tools with UCLA’s licenses', an eligibility limit on licensed tools (P92 for licensed tools).
units.anchor: only students 18 and older can use these tools with UCLA’s licenses
units.fit_note: States who may use the licensed tools (age 18+), not that students must use them.

units.why: Says 'This guide builds on a teaching guide created by CEILS in collaboration with previous campus teaching and learning organizations', describing how the guide was made (P84).
units.anchor: This guide builds on a teaching guide created by CEILS

documents.title: Creating a Generative AI Policy for Your Course
tiers: Limited use of AI in class with citation
documents.summary: Excerpt of the TLC guide focused on how instructors create a course GenAI policy: guiding questions, three sample statements, and where to go for suspected misconduct.
documents.stance_why: The page gives guiding questions and three example syllabus statements 'that instructors could include or adapt', and sets no university rule, so the decision is delegated to instructors with tiered options.

units.why: Says the resource guides instructors 'on deciding whether to implement tools in courses', placing the decision with the instructor (P04).
units.anchor: guidance on deciding whether to implement tools in courses

units.why: The third question asks how students 'document their interactions with GenAI (e.g., cite it where relevant, attach appendices with chat logs)'. P26 fits (logs) with a fit note since it covers citing too.

units.fit_note: Framed as a question for instructors and mixes citation with chat-log appendices.

units.why: The same question asks how students 'document their own contributions that do not involve AI' (version history, handwritten outlines), process evidence (P26).
